description_full: Himalaya Shipping Ltd. provides dry bulk shipping services worldwide. The company serves major commodity trading, commodity and energy transition, and multi-modal transport companies. As of December 31, 2024, it owned and operated through a fleet of 12 Newcastlemax dry bulk vessels, each with capacity in the range of 210,000 dead weight tons. Himalaya Shipping Ltd. was incorporated in 2021 and is based in Hamilton, Bermuda.
ceo_bio: Mr. Lars-Christian  Svensen | Contracted Chief Executive Officer | Age 39
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 3 people. Revenue per employee of $44.0M ranks in the top quartile among Industrials peers, improving at 89%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Stock-based compensation of $67K per employee reflects an ownership culture.
financial_summary: Himalaya Shipping Ltd. is a small-cap industrials business with a $728M market cap on $132M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +89% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 6.7× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 1.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.6%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 28% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 4.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Critical Analysis: Himalaya Shipping (NYSE:HSHP) & Genco Shipping & Trading (NYSE:GNK)

sect: Its 52% operating margin runs 43pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 4.70x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 155% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 21% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 43% and a beta of 0.90, it moves roughly with the market.
About $7.6M trades a day, enough to build a position.
val: The price sits above its blended-model fair value of $3.33 (margin of safety -364%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 22%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 13.7 vs 23.3 and EV/EBITDA 10.3 vs 13.3 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an EBIT/EV of 5.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $16.90 on average, 10% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.3%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.54).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.92x.
ROE of 11% is amplified by 5.3x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.2% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 6.7x net debt to EBITDA ($32.4M of cash against $689.2M of debt), and interest cover is thin at 1.3x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.10 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 89.5% over 3 years.
own: Insiders own 28.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 58%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 2 sales over the past year, net $5.5M sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.6% (21.8% in dividends, less 2.1% of net share issuance).
It pays out 101% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 3 employees, each generates about $44.0M of revenue, 119.7x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 89.5% a year.
